prime.problem: A warehouse question like "Q3 net revenue for EMEA" can be answered by several perfectly valid queries that return different numbers. Nothing errors, so an agent that only writes SQL hands back one of them with full confidence, and nobody can tell which reading it picked.
prime.fits: First card of the data-agents case study. You already have the agent loop and the ten-layer ownership map; this card points both at a warehouse and shows which layer has to carry the weight when the tool never fails loudly.
prime.goal: Explain why a data agent is more than text-to-SQL, place a real data agent's parts on the ten-layer map, and say what has to exist before its answer counts as verified.

attend: In the Q3 example, why do all eight queries succeed, and what would have to exist for one of them to fail?
The Tuesday run's checker catches a false claim by re-running pytest. What is the closest thing a data agent's checker can re-run, and why is it weaker?
Which of the eight loop steps would a one-shot text-to-SQL system skip, and which failure mode does each skipped step let through?
Why must permissions be checked before context retrieval, not just filtered out of the final answer?
In OpenAI's agent as he reports it, which two layers turn a number into a checked answer, and which layer is not described at all?

must: The warehouse accepts any well-formed query → several readings of one question all execute and return plausible numbers → no exit code separates right from wrong → correctness has to come from definitions (metric contracts, catalog, pipeline code), not from running the SQL again

Meaning is spread across metric definitions, lineage, catalog notes, code and people → a schema gives only shape → the agent must assemble the smallest evidence set that pins the reading, or ask → otherwise it silently picks a definition ("right metric name, wrong definition")

A wrong reading can't be caught by re-execution → the answer must ship with a receipt (question as understood, definition, tables, filters, SQL, assumptions, denied data) → a human or an eval can see which choice was made → evals compare executed results against golden results, not SQL text

Conversational access must not create new authority → pass-through permissions mean the agent acts with the asker's rights → checks must run before retrieval and execution, because retrieved context and the summary can leak too
elevated: Tool surface size: OpenAI's post (as he reports it) found the full overlapping tool set confused the agent, so tools were restricted and consolidated → ByteByteGo's account adds that reliability improved after the cut (from around 40 tools) → fewer, non-overlapping tools is a reliability lever, not just tidiness
reference: his five broad layers: meaning, context, governance, execution, verification
the six OpenAI context layers by name: table usage, human annotations, code enrichment, institutional knowledge, memory, runtime context
OpenAI platform scale as reported in Part 2: over 3.5k internal users, over 600 PB, 70k datasets
the exact wording of Luo et al.'s level names (none, assistance, partial, conditional, high, full)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences why a data agent is not text-to-SQL, using the Q3 EMEA question. Or draw the eight-step loop and mark which step text-to-SQL covers and which steps catch meaning errors.
checklist: the SQL nearly always runs, so syntax is not where answers go wrong; meaning is (metric, entity, time, table)
there is no executable oracle like pytest; the check is a definition that lives outside the warehouse
the agent resolves meaning from assembled context or asks, rather than picking silently
permissions are part of the execution path (pass-through), checked before retrieval
the answer ships with a receipt so a wrong reading is at least visible
evals execute and compare results, not SQL strings

retrieve.q: Explain why a data agent's answer can be wrong even when the generated SQL is syntactically and logically valid.
answer: the query can hit the wrong table (grain, staleness, excluded population, deprecated)
the metric word can map to the wrong definition
a legal join can be semantically wrong
none of these raise an error, so execution success says nothing about meaning

retrieve.q: Walk the Q3 EMEA question through the eight-step loop. At which step should the fiscal-versus-calendar choice be settled, and what should appear in the receipt about it?
answer: intent and metric resolution decides or asks about the time window
context assembly supplies the evidence (a fiscal calendar definition, the metric contract)
the plan and execution use the chosen window
validation checks the result makes sense
the receipt states the window used as an assumption, alongside definition, tables, filters and SQL

retrieve.q: Your team must pick: ask the user a clarifying question every time a metric is ambiguous, or apply a documented default and state it in the receipt. What does each cost, and when would you pick each?
answer: asking: slower, interrupts the user, but avoids a silently wrong reading
default plus receipt: fast, but only safe if the user actually reads the stated assumption
pick asking when readings diverge a lot or stakes are high (finance close)
pick defaults when a governed definition exists and the receipt is shown; his posts report OpenAI's agent asks when unclear and applies sensible defaults if the user doesn't answer

retrieve.q: Why does golden-SQL string matching make a poor eval for a data agent, and what does the eval shape he describes do instead?
answer: different SQL can be equally correct, and similar SQL can return a wrong result
his described shape executes the generated SQL and compares its results with the expected results
a grader then returns a score and an explanation

compare.q: On the Tuesday run the failure sits in the context layer (compaction dropped the exit code) and the operator loop catches it. For the Q3 question, which layer holds the failure when the agent picks the wrong "EMEA", and can the operator loop catch it the same way?
answer: Q3 failure sits in context (missing definition) or intent resolution, not in execution
Tuesday: the operator loop re-runs a world check (pytest) and gets exit 1
Q3: re-running the query reproduces the wrong number; the operator loop needs a golden result or a human definition
so for data agents, layer 9 depends on layers 5 and 8 having real definitions and permissions to check against

compare.q: Measuring a coding agent uses hidden tests as the verdict. What replaces hidden tests for a data agent, and how does each verdict fail?
answer: coding: hidden tests executed in the repo; fails when tests are weak or missing
data: golden question–answer pairs whose expected results are compared after execution; fails when the golden value is stale or the definition changed
both need repeats and error bars; data evals also go stale because the data moves (the changing-data card)

predict.q: Finance publishes a single governed net_revenue metric in a semantic layer, with region and fiscal calendar built in. Of the eight readings in the worked example, how many can the agent still produce through that metric, and which loop step loses most of its work?
predict.answer: If the agent must go through the governed metric, essentially one reading per definition remains: the eight collapse to the metric's own choices. Intent and metric resolution (and much of context assembly) shrinks to "map the words to this metric". The remaining risks move elsewhere: the agent bypassing the metric and querying raw tables, the metric definition itself being wrong or stale, and permissions. That's why he treats the foundation as part of the agent (next card).

apply.task: Run python3 code/data-agent-anatomy.py. Then add a fourth hidden choice: include or exclude accounts flagged as test traffic (add a is_test column set for about 1 in 10 accounts). Re-run and count the readings, then write the receipt line that would tell a reader which of the readings was used.
apply.done: The script prints 16 readings, all with status ok. The original eight values reappear unchanged as the "include" half, and the spread widens: with the hint's draw the answers run from $878.6k to $1,201.4k, 1.37× instead of 1.16×.
apply.hint: Add is_test DEFAULT 0 to the accounts table and name the columns in its INSERT. After the orders loop, loop over the 80 accounts and set is_test = 1 when rng.random() < 0.1, so earlier draws don't shift. Then add TEST = {'include': '1=1', 'exclude': 'a.is_test = 0'} to itertools.product and the WHERE clause.
